## Background

@holland1990dutch introduced the **Dutch Identity** — a result about the
mathematical structure that any unidimensional IRT model imposes on the joint
distribution of dichotomous item responses. The key insight is that the
*manifest* (unconditional) probability of a response pattern $\mathbf{x} =
(x_1, \ldots, x_J) \in \{0,1\}^J$ can be written as an exponential family
whose sufficient statistics are functions of the item responses. For large tests
with smooth item response functions (IRFs), this reduces to a strikingly simple
approximation:

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) \approx \alpha + \sum_{j=1}^{J} \beta_j x_j + \frac{1}{2}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{J} \gamma_j x_j\right)^{\!2}$$

This is log-quadratic in the $x_j$, requires only $2J + 1$ parameters regardless
of $J$, and makes precise predictions about the structure of second-order
interactions between items. The sections below work through the implications one
step at a time, using IRW datasets to make each idea concrete.

::: {.callout-note}
All figures use pre-computed results from `dutch_identity_compute.R`. The
dataset used in Sections 1–3 is **`r s1_3$table_name`**
($J = `r s1_3$J`$ items, $N = `r format(s1_3$N, big.mark=",")`$ respondents,
computed `r format(date_run, "%B %Y")`).
:::

---

## Section 1: The manifest probabilities directly

For a test of $J$ binary items, a respondent's answers define a response pattern
$\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^J$. There are $2^J$ possible patterns, each occurring
with manifest probability $p(\mathbf{x})$. Before modeling, it is worth asking:
what do these probabilities actually look like? Most patterns are extremely rare;
a handful dominate. @holland1990dutch motivates the loglinear approach precisely
because the $p(\mathbf{x})$ are too numerous and sparse to model directly for
large $J$.

For $J \leq 10$ items and $N \geq 2{,}000$ respondents the full distribution is
enumerable. Below we tabulate every $2^J$ pattern and display the empirical
$p(\mathbf{x})$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-manifest-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of empirical manifest probabilities across all 2^J response patterns (log scale). Most patterns are never observed (grey); a few common patterns carry most of the probability mass. Hover over a point to see its response pattern."

patterns <- s1_3$patterns |>
  arrange(desc(count)) |>
  mutate(
    rank        = row_number(),
    p_obs       = count / s1_3$N,
    observed    = count > 0,
    pattern_str = apply(pick(all_of(s1_3$item_cols)), 1, paste, collapse = ""),
    tooltip     = paste0(
      "Pattern: ", pattern_str,
      "<br>p(x): ", signif(p_obs, 3),
      "<br>Count: ", count
    )
  )

n_observed   <- sum(patterns$observed)
n_unobserved <- sum(!patterns$observed)

p <- ggplot(patterns, aes(x = rank, y = p_obs, colour = observed, text = tooltip)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = irw_blue, "FALSE" = irw_grey),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Observed", "FALSE" = "Never seen"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  labs(
    x = "Pattern rank (most to least common)",
    y = "Empirical p(x)  [log scale]"
  )

plotly::ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") |>
  plotly::layout(
    annotations = list(list(
      text      = paste0(n_observed, " of ", 2^s1_3$J,
                         " patterns observed; ", n_unobserved, " never appeared."),
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
      x = 0, y = -0.12,
      xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top",
      font = list(size = 11, color = "grey50")
    ))
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-score-dist
#| fig-cap: "Total probability mass at each sum score k = Σ xⱼ. Patterns within each score group contribute additively."
#| fig-height: 4

patterns |>
  filter(observed) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(total), y = p_obs, fill = p_obs)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#d1e5f0", high = irw_blue) +
  labs(
    x       = "Total score k",
    y       = "p(x)",
    caption = "Each bar is the total probability mass at that score level."
  )
```

**What to notice.** Probability mass is extremely concentrated: the most common
pattern can account for a large share of the total. The long tail of near-zero
patterns means a $2^J$-parameter saturated model is hopeless — most cells have
zero or one observation. This motivates the loglinear parameterisation in
Section 2.

The [bits-per-item vignette](bits_per_item.qmd#answer-patterns) uses this same
distribution to count how much a test tells you about a person: the entropy of
p(**x**), minus the part that is chance rather than differences between
people. It also shows that the independence model of Section 2 falls short by
exactly the information that items share.

---

## Section 2: Log-manifest probabilities and the independence baseline

Under item *independence* — no latent variable, no associations — $\log
p(\mathbf{x})$ is a linear function of the item responses:

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha + \sum_{j=1}^{J} \beta_j x_j$$

This **independence loglinear model** has $J + 1$ parameters. It is equivalent
to a Poisson regression of pattern counts on the $J$ binary item predictors.
When it fits, all structure in the data is captured by item marginals alone.

Any IRT model implies that $\log p(\mathbf{x})$ *deviates* from this baseline —
the latent variable induces positive associations among items that the
main-effects model misses. Plotting observed versus fitted $\log p(\mathbf{x})$
makes those deviations visible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-independence-fit
#| fig-cap: "Observed vs. fitted log p(x) under the independence loglinear model. Points on the diagonal are fully explained by item marginals; points below the line are more probable than independence predicts (positive local dependence)."
#| fig-height: 4.5

plot_dat <- patterns |>
  filter(observed) |>
  mutate(
    residual = log_p_obs - log_p_ind,
    tooltip  = paste0(
      "Pattern: ", pattern_str,
      "<br>Observed log p(x): ",  round(log_p_obs, 3),
      "<br>Fitted log p(x): ",    round(log_p_ind, 3),
      "<br>Residual: ",           round(residual,  3)
    )
  )

r2_ind <- cor(plot_dat$log_p_obs, plot_dat$log_p_ind, use = "complete.obs")^2

p <- ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x = log_p_ind, y = log_p_obs, text = tooltip)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = irw_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(size = p_obs), colour = irw_blue, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 5), name = "p(x)", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted log p(x)  [independence model]",
    y = "Observed log p(x)"
  )

plotly::ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") |>
  plotly::layout(
    annotations = list(list(
      text      = paste0("R² = ", round(r2_ind, 3), ". Hover to see the response pattern for each point."),
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
      x = 0, y = -0.12,
      xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top",
      font = list(size = 11, color = "grey50")
    ))
  )
```

**What to notice.** Systematic curvature away from the diagonal — especially
for extreme total-score patterns — signals that main effects alone are not
enough. The points that deviate most are those where all or nearly all items are
answered the same way: item correlation inflates these relative to the
independence prediction. This is exactly the second-order structure that
@holland1990dutch formalises.

---

## Section 3: Fitting the second-order exponential model

The full **second-order exponential (SOE) model** augments the independence
model with all $\binom{J}{2}$ pairwise interaction terms:

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha + \sum_j \beta_j x_j + \sum_{j < k} \gamma_{jk}\, x_j x_k$$

This is still a Poisson GLM, now with $1 + J + \binom{J}{2}$ parameters. The
$J \times J$ matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ (with $\Gamma_{jk} = \gamma_{jk}$ and
$\Gamma_{jj} = 0$) encodes all pairwise item associations after removing main
effects.

The Dutch Identity [@holland1990dutch, Theorem 1] predicts that
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is *approximately rank-1*: $\Gamma_{jk} \approx \gamma_j
\gamma_k$. Under this constraint, the interaction structure collapses to:

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) \approx \alpha + \sum_j \beta_j' x_j + \frac{1}{2}\!\left(\sum_j \gamma_j x_j\right)^{\!2}$$

the **restricted log-quadratic** model ($1 + 2J$ parameters). We fit all three
models and compare.

### Model comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bic
#| tbl-cap: "Log-likelihood and BIC for three nested loglinear models, all fitted by Poisson maximum likelihood to the same table of 2^J pattern counts with zero cells included. The restricted log-quadratic uses 2J + 1 parameters; the full SOE uses 1 + J + J(J-1)/2. BIC uses n = N respondents for every row."

s1_3$bic_table |>
  mutate(
    across(c(Log_lik, BIC), \(x) round(x, 1)),
    BIC_delta = round(BIC - min(BIC), 1)
  ) |>
  rename(`ΔBIC vs. best` = BIC_delta, `Log-lik` = Log_lik) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

All three models are fitted to the same $2^J$ pattern counts — zero cells
included — by Poisson maximum likelihood, so the log-likelihoods are on one
scale, and BIC uses $n = N = `r format(s1_3$bic_n, big.mark=",")`$ respondents
for every row. Each model has a free intercept, so its fitted counts sum to $N$;
the multinomial log-likelihoods therefore differ from the Poisson ones by a
constant that is the same for all three
(`r paste(sprintf("%.1f", s1_3$ll_multinomial), collapse = ", ")` for
independence, log-quadratic and SOE respectively).

The three models are nested: independence is the log-quadratic with $\gamma = 0$,
and the log-quadratic is the full SOE with $\Gamma_{jk}$ forced to
$\gamma_j \gamma_k$. The log-likelihoods must therefore increase down the table,
and they do. The rank-1 fit is by direct Poisson maximum likelihood rather than
by a GLM, since $\gamma$ enters only through $(\mathbf{x}'\gamma)^2$ and so is
identified only up to sign; of
`r s1_3$rq_convergence$n_starts` starting values,
`r s1_3$rq_convergence$n_at_best` reached the reported optimum.

The key question is whether the restricted log-quadratic — which enforces rank-1
structure on $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ — captures most of the association signal
while using only $1 + 2J$ parameters instead of $1 + J + \binom{J}{2}$. It
captures nearly all of it: the rank-1 model recovers
**`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$rq_gap_share)`** of the
independence-to-SOE log-likelihood gap,
$(\ell_{\text{rq}} - \ell_{\text{ind}})/(\ell_{\text{soe}} - \ell_{\text{ind}})$,
with `r s1_3$bic_table$Parameters[3] - s1_3$bic_table$Parameters[2]` fewer
parameters. BIC still prefers the full SOE, but only by
`r sprintf("%.1f", round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[2], 1) - round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[3], 1))`
— small beside the
`r sprintf("%.1f", round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[1], 1) - round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[3], 1))`
that separates independence from the SOE.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model-fit
#| fig-cap: "Observed vs. fitted log-probability for each of the three loglinear models across all observed response patterns. Points on the dashed diagonal indicate perfect fit; scatter above the diagonal means the model over-predicts that pattern."
#| fig-height: 3.5

fit_df <- s1_3$patterns |>
  filter(!is.na(log_p_obs)) |>
  select(log_p_obs, log_p_ind, log_p_rq, log_p_soe) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(log_p_ind, log_p_rq, log_p_soe),
    names_to  = "model",
    values_to = "log_p_fit"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(log_p_fit)) |>
  mutate(model = factor(recode(model,
    log_p_ind = "Independence",
    log_p_rq  = "Log-quadratic\n(rank-1 Γ)",
    log_p_soe = "Full SOE"
  ), levels = c("Independence", "Log-quadratic\n(rank-1 Γ)", "Full SOE")))

ggplot(fit_df, aes(x = log_p_obs, y = log_p_fit)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5, colour = irw_blue) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    x       = "Observed log-probability",
    y       = "Fitted log-probability",
    caption = paste0(
      nrow(s1_3$patterns |> filter(!is.na(log_p_obs))),
      " observed response patterns from ", s1_3$table_name, "."
    )
  )
```

### Structure of the Γ matrix

```{r}
#| label: fig-gamma-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Heatmap of the J×J interaction matrix Γ from the full SOE model. Under the Dutch Identity, off-diagonal entries should follow a rank-1 pattern γⱼγₖ — all rows should look like rescaled versions of each other."
#| fig-height: 4

gmat      <- s1_3$gamma_matrix
gmat_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(gmat)) |>
  rename(item1 = Var1, item2 = Var2, gamma = Freq) |>
  filter(item1 != item2)

ggplot(gmat_long, aes(x = item2, y = item1, fill = gamma)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = irw_red, mid = "white", high = irw_blue,
    midpoint = 0, name = "γⱼₖ"
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid  = element_blank()
  )
```

Under a rank-1 $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, every row is a scalar multiple of every
other — the color profile across columns should look identical up to intensity.
Systematic blocks or rows that deviate from the common pattern signal local
dependence that a single latent factor cannot absorb.

### Is Γ rank-1?

The Dutch Identity's prediction about $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ concerns the
**off-diagonal** entries only. Expanding the quadratic term and using
$x_j^2 = x_j$ for binary items,

$$\frac{1}{2}\!\left(\sum_j \gamma_j x_j\right)^{\!2}
  = \frac{1}{2}\sum_j \gamma_j^2 x_j \;+\; \sum_{j<k} \gamma_j \gamma_k x_j x_k,$$

so the squared terms are absorbed into the main effects and the prediction is
$\Gamma_{jk} \approx \gamma_j \gamma_k$ for $j \neq k$. The diagonal is free; in
the SOE fit $\Gamma_{jj} = 0$ by construction, because there is no $x_j^2$ term
to estimate.

That construction has a consequence worth stating before any eigenvalues are
plotted: $\operatorname{trace}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}) = 0$, so the eigenvalues of
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ must sum to zero. Large negative eigenvalues are forced by
the zero diagonal and say nothing about dimensionality. Indeed for *any*
$\boldsymbol{\gamma}$, the exactly rank-1 structure
$\boldsymbol{\gamma}\boldsymbol{\gamma}' - \operatorname{diag}(\gamma_j^2)$ has
at most one positive eigenvalue, from which
$\lambda_1 / \sum_j |\lambda_j| \le 1/2$ with equality precisely when one
eigenvalue is positive. A scree plot of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is therefore not a
test of the rank-1 prediction, and "the leading eigenvalue explains 50% of the
absolute eigenvalue mass" is the *ceiling* of that statistic rather than a
shortfall. An earlier version of this page read it the other way around.

The diagnostic that does test the prediction leaves the diagonal alone: fit the
best rank-1 structure to the off-diagonal entries, minimising
$\sum_{j<k} w_{jk}(\Gamma_{jk} - g_j g_k)^2$ with weights
$w_{jk} = 1/\mathrm{SE}(\Gamma_{jk})^2$ from the SOE fit, and ask what share of
the off-diagonal (weighted) sum of squares it explains.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gamma-rank1-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Off-diagonal entries of Γ from the full SOE fit against γⱼγₖ from the fitted restricted log-quadratic model, with the 45° line. Error bars are ±1 SE of the SOE coefficient. This is the direct check of the Dutch Identity's prediction; the diagonal plays no part in it."
#| fig-height: 3.8

sc <- s1_3$gamma_rank1$scatter

ggplot(sc, aes(x = gamma_pred, y = gamma_soe)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = irw_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = gamma_soe - se, ymax = gamma_soe + se),
                width = 0, colour = irw_grey, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = irw_blue, size = 2.4, alpha = 0.9) +
  labs(x = expression(gamma[j] * gamma[k] ~ "(restricted log-quadratic)"),
       y = expression(Gamma[jk] ~ "(full SOE)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gamma-scree
#| fig-cap: "Eigenvalues of Γ (bars), with the eigenvalues of an exactly rank-1 reference structure γγ′ with its diagonal zeroed (points). Both sets are constrained to sum to zero by the zero diagonal, so the negative eigenvalues are not evidence against rank-1 — the rank-1 ideal has them too."
#| fig-height: 3.5

eig_df <- tibble(
  component  = seq_along(s1_3$eigenvalues),
  eigenvalue = s1_3$eigenvalues,
  reference  = s1_3$gamma_rank1$reference_eigen
)

ggplot(eig_df, aes(x = component, y = eigenvalue)) +
  geom_col(fill = irw_blue, alpha = 0.7, width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(y = reference), colour = irw_red, size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_len(s1_3$J)) +
  labs(
    x       = "Component",
    y       = "Eigenvalue of Γ",
    caption = paste0(
      "Bars: observed Γ. Points: exactly rank-1 reference. Both sum to zero ",
      "by construction (trace Γ = 0)."
    )
  )
```

**What to notice.** The restricted log-quadratic model ($1 + 2J$ parameters)
closes `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$rq_gap_share)` of the gap between the
independence model and the full SOE ($1 + J + \binom{J}{2}$ parameters) — the
Dutch Identity's economy claim, holding up here.

The rank-1 claim about $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ itself is a separate question, and
it needs a reference point: a test this short at this $N$ will never return an
exactly rank-1 $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, so a high share proves nothing on its own.
We simulate `r s1_3$gamma_rank1$n_boot` sets of pattern counts from the fitted
restricted log-quadratic model at the same $N$ — a world where the Dutch
Identity holds exactly — refit the SOE, and recompute the diagnostic. Under that
null the weighted off-diagonal share has median
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$gamma_rank1$boot_summary$share_w_median)`
and 95% of replicates fall in
[`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$gamma_rank1$boot_summary$share_w_lo)`,
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$gamma_rank1$boot_summary$share_w_hi)`].

The observed share is
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$gamma_rank1$rank1_weighted$share)`
(`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$gamma_rank1$rank1_unweighted$share)`
unweighted), below every one of the
`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$n_boot` null replicates. So $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ here is
**not** rank-1, and the departure is not a sampling artefact. @fig-gamma-rank1-scatter
shows where it lives:
`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$n_resid_z_gt_3` of the
`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$n_offdiag` off-diagonal entries sit more than three standard
errors from $\gamma_j\gamma_k$, the largest being
`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$worst_resid$item1`–`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$worst_resid$item2`
at `r sprintf("%.1f", s1_3$gamma_rank1$worst_resid$z)` SE. That is local
dependence between particular item pairs — structure a single latent dimension
cannot absorb.

Note also that the eigenvalue count has no power to detect this.
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ has exactly
`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$eigen_facts$n_positive` positive eigenvalue, which is the
rank-1 prediction — but so do
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * s1_3$gamma_rank1$boot_prop_one_positive)` of the null
replicates, and so does any rank-1 matrix with a zeroed diagonal. Passing that
check is not evidence.

The two findings are not in conflict, and the combination is the useful lesson.
Rank-1 is rejected as a description of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ while remaining an
excellent *predictive* approximation: the five extra interaction parameters the
SOE spends on the non-rank-1 structure buy it only
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - s1_3$rq_gap_share))` of the likelihood gap.
Statistical rejection and practical adequacy are answers to different questions,
and at $N = `r format(s1_3$N, big.mark=",")`$ a real but small departure is
detectable without being important for prediction.

### Is this table unusual?

Everything above concerns one instrument. The economy claim — that a single
dimension closes almost all of the gap between independence and the full SOE —
is worth asking of the corpus, because on one table it could be a property of
these five items rather than of item response data.

So we ask it of every IRW table that admits the same three fits: binary items,
$`r gs_sum$j_min` \le J \le `r gs_sum$j_max`$, and enough respondents to
populate $2^J$ cells. That is `r gs_sum$n_tables` tables. For each one we fit
the same nested triple to its own pattern counts and form the same ratio, but
out of sample: five-fold cross-validation over respondents, scoring each
held-out fold under models fitted on the other four. In-sample the ratio is
bounded in $[0,1]$ and inflated when $J$ is small, which would flatter the
restricted model exactly where it has least to explain. Out of sample it is
bounded by neither, so a few tables land slightly above 1.

Fitted cell probabilities are floored at $1/(10 N_{\text{train}})$ before
scoring, because a single held-out respondent landing in a numerically empty
cell would otherwise dominate its fold — a fact about an empty cell, not about
overfitting. That choice is immaterial in aggregate (the median moves from
`r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_out_raw)` unfloored to
`r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_out)` floored) but not for every table: it shifts
`r gs_sum$n_floor_moves` of the `r gs_sum$n_usable` by more than 0.05, at most
`r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$max_floor_move)`. Both versions are in the CSV.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gapshare-corpus
#| fig-cap: "Held-out gap share for every IRW table admitting the three fits, against the number of items. Each blue point is one table. The dashed line is the median over all tables — the 96.3% quoted below. Red segments are per-J medians, which is where the decline with J shows up. The circled point is the table analysed in this vignette. A value of 1 means one latent dimension captures all of the pairwise association the full SOE finds."
#| fig-height: 4.2

gs_u    <- gs[gs$share_out_usable, ]
gs_this <- gs_u[gs_u$table == s1_3$table_name, ]
set.seed(1)   # fixed jitter, so the figure is stable across renders
gs_u$xj <- gs_u$J + runif(nrow(gs_u), -0.14, 0.14)

ggplot(gs_u, aes(x = xj, y = share_out_floor)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = gs_sum$med_out, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = irw_grey) +
  annotate("text", x = gs_sum$j_max + 0.42, y = gs_sum$med_out,
           label = sprintf("median %.3f", gs_sum$med_out),
           hjust = 1, vjust = -0.6, size = 3.2, colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = irw_blue, size = 1.9) +
  geom_segment(data = gs_sum$by_j,
               aes(x = J - 0.32, xend = J + 0.32,
                   y = share_out_floor, yend = share_out_floor),
               colour = irw_red, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = gs_this, aes(x = J, y = share_out_floor),
             shape = 21, size = 3.6, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "grey15", fill = NA) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = gs_sum$j_min:gs_sum$j_max,
                     limits = c(gs_sum$j_min - 0.45, gs_sum$j_max + 0.45)) +
  labs(x = "Number of items (J)", y = "Held-out gap share",
       caption = paste0(
         "Dashed: median over all ", gs_sum$n_usable,
         " tables. Red: per-J medians.\n",
         "Circled: ", s1_3$table_name, "."
       )) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = irw_grey))
```

**What to notice.** The dashed line is the headline: the median table gives one
dimension `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gs_sum$med_out)` of the gap (IQR
[`r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$q1_out)`, `r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$q3_out)`]). The
circled point is this vignette's table, at
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gs_sum$this_out)` — above the median but well inside
the cloud of its $J = `r s1_3$J`$ neighbours, so ordinary rather than
exceptional. In absolute terms the residual is small too: across tables the
restricted model is worth a median
`r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_rq_nats)` nats per held-out respondent over
independence, the full SOE `r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_soe_nats)`, and the
median table's own difference between the two is
`r sprintf("%.4f", gs_sum$med_beyond_nats)` nats — about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * gs_sum$med_beyond_nats / gs_sum$med_rq_nats)` of what
the first dimension buys. The economy claim is a property of these data broadly,
not of this instrument.

It does decay with $J$, monotonically over most of the range, from
`r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$by_j$share_out_floor[1])` at $J = `r gs_sum$by_j$J[1]`$
to
`r sprintf("%.2f", tail(gs_sum$by_j$share_out_floor, 1))` at
$J = `r tail(gs_sum$by_j$J, 1)`$. Whether that is about item count or about what
long instruments measure, these data cannot say: more items means more pairs
that *can* depart from rank-1, and it also means instruments that sprawl across
facets. The low outliers favour the second reading — the worst cases are item
sets that were never indicators of one trait, such as a battery asking which
*sources* someone used for COVID information, or a short subscale that mixes
material deprivation with supervision. They look like separate clusters because
they are.

Two cautions. The ratio's denominator can be small: for `r gs_sum$n_thin` of the
`r gs_sum$n_usable` tables the full SOE beats independence by under 0.05 nats
per respondent, and a low share there means there was little to explain rather
than that one dimension failed. More importantly, this is a share of
*second-order* association. The SOE is itself a restricted model — no three-way
or higher interactions — so a table at 96% has one dimension capturing 96% of
what the pairwise model captures, which is silent about dependence neither model
can see. The per-table numbers, the exclusions and the diagnostics are in
`vignettes/dutchdata/gapshare_summary.md`.

---

## Section 4: The γₖ diagnostic for the Rasch model

@holland1990dutch Corollary 2 gives a striking prediction about the Rasch model.
If ability $\theta \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, the probability of obtaining total
score $k$ is:

$$\log \pi_k \approx C + \mu(k - \bar{y}_+) + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}(k - \bar{y}_+)^2$$

where $\bar{y}_+ = \sum_j \bar{p}_j$ is the expected total score at the mean
ability. In other words, $\log \pi_k$ is a *quadratic* function of $k$, centred
on $\bar{y}_+$. Systematic deviations indicate either non-normality of the
ability distribution or Rasch misfit.

We compare two IRW datasets, chosen on the quantity these figures actually
show — the $R^2$ of the quadratic fit to $\log \pi_k$. One where that quadratic
holds closely (**`r s4$good_rasch$table_name`**, $J = `r s4$good_rasch$J`$,
$N = `r format(s4$good_rasch$N, big.mark=",")`$,
$R^2 = `r round(s4$good_rasch$r2_quad, 3)`$) and one where it does not
(**`r s4$poor_rasch$table_name`**, $J = `r s4$poor_rasch$J`$,
$N = `r format(s4$poor_rasch$N, big.mark=",")`$,
$R^2 = `r round(s4$poor_rasch$r2_quad, 3)`$).

Rasch misfit itself is quoted per response, $\Delta\ell / (NJ)$ for the 2PL
against the Rasch model: `r signif(s4$good_rasch$ll_diff_per_resp, 2)` and
`r signif(s4$poor_rasch$ll_diff_per_resp, 2)` respectively. Raw $\Delta\ell$ is
not comparable across datasets — it grows with the number of responses, so a
larger dataset looks like worse Rasch fit for free, and the raw values here
(`r round(s4$good_rasch$ll_diff, 1)` and `r round(s4$poor_rasch$ll_diff, 1)`)
would overstate the contrast by a wide margin.

```{r}
#| label: plot-gk-fn
#| echo: false

plot_gk <- function(gk_data) {
  ggplot(gk_data, aes(x = k, y = gamma_k)) +
    geom_point(colour = irw_blue, size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(aes(y = gamma_k_fitted), colour = irw_red,
              linewidth = 0.9) +
    labs(
      x       = "Total score k",
      y       = expression(log~pi[k]),
      caption = "Red curve: fitted quadratic."
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gamma-k-good
#| fig-cap: "Total-score log-frequencies for the dataset with the closest quadratic fit. Points follow a smooth quadratic, consistent with Holland's Corollary 2."
#| fig-height: 4

plot_gk(s4$good_rasch$gamma_k_data)
```

The quadratic $R^2$ is `r round(s4$good_rasch$r2_quad, 3)` for this dataset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gamma-k-poor
#| fig-cap: "Total-score log-frequencies for the dataset with the worst quadratic fit. Deviations from the quadratic suggest a non-normal ability distribution or non-constant discrimination."
#| fig-height: 4

plot_gk(s4$poor_rasch$gamma_k_data)
```

The quadratic $R^2$ is `r round(s4$poor_rasch$r2_quad, 3)` for this dataset.

**What to notice.** When Rasch holds, $\log \pi_k$ traces a clean inverted
parabola. Deviations can take two forms: (1) a sharp peak at the mode with thin
tails, suggesting a more leptokurtic ability distribution; or (2) asymmetry or a
kink, consistent with varying item discriminations. The $R^2$ from the quadratic
regression is a quick, model-free diagnostic, but it is a comparative one rather
than a test against a fixed cutoff. Across the
`r nrow(s4$rasch_meta)` datasets screened here it ranges from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(s4$rasch_meta$r2_quad))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(s4$rasch_meta$r2_quad))`; the top of that range is about
as quadratic as real total-score distributions get, and values below roughly
0.95 are worth investigating.

The two diagnostics need not agree, and here they do not. Corollary 2 is a joint
prediction about Rasch fit *and* normality of the ability distribution, so either
can break it. **`r s4$good_rasch$table_name`** happens to be best on both counts
— highest quadratic $R^2$ and the smallest per-response 2PL gain in the set. But
**`r s4$poor_rasch$table_name`**, with much the worst quadratic fit, is only
middling on Rasch misfit per response
(`r signif(s4$poor_rasch$ll_diff_per_resp, 2)`, against a worst-in-set
`r signif(max(s4$rasch_meta$ll_diff_per_resp), 2)` for
**`r s4$rasch_meta$table_name[which.max(s4$rasch_meta$ll_diff_per_resp)]`**).
What its $\log \pi_k$ curve is flagging is the shape of the score distribution,
not non-constant discrimination — which is the caveat in the box at the foot of
this page, met in the data.

---

## Section 5: Dimensionality via second-order interaction matrices

Holland ([-@holland1990dutch], Section 3.3) shows that for a $D$-dimensional IRT
model, the **off-diagonal** structure of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is approximately
of rank $D$ — and, as in Section 3, this is an approximation that sharpens as
$J$ grows, about the off-diagonals with the diagonal left free. It is tempting
to read it as "count the non-negligible eigenvalues of
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$", but that reading does not work: the SOE fit forces
$\Gamma_{jj} = 0$, so the eigenvalues sum to zero and the negative ones are an
artefact of the constraint rather than a count of dimensions. Section 3 gives the
diagnostic that does work, and shows that even the $D = 1$ case has to be judged
against a simulated rank-1 reference rather than by eye. So this section stays
with the standard approach — eigenvalues of the inter-item correlation matrix,
whose diagonal is 1 and which is a different, conventional setup — and treats
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ only through Section 3's machinery.

We use **`r s5$unidim$table_name`** ($J = `r s5$unidim$J`$) as the
unidimensional candidate and **`r s5$multidim$table_name`**
($J = `r s5$multidim$J`$) as the more complex one.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scree-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Scree plots of inter-item correlation matrix eigenvalues. A sharply dominant first eigenvalue indicates unidimensionality; multiple eigenvalues above 1 indicate multidimensionality."
#| fig-height: 5.5

make_scree_df <- function(dim_result, label) {
  tibble(
    label      = label,
    component  = seq_along(dim_result$cor_eigval),
    eigenvalue = dim_result$cor_eigval,
    pct_var    = dim_result$cor_eigval / sum(dim_result$cor_eigval)
  )
}

scree_df <- bind_rows(
  make_scree_df(
    s5$unidim,
    paste0("Unidimensional: ", s5$unidim$table_name, " (J=", s5$unidim$J, ")")
  ),
  make_scree_df(
    s5$multidim,
    paste0("Complex: ", s5$multidim$table_name, " (J=", s5$multidim$J, ")")
  )
) |> filter(component <= 10)

ggplot(scree_df, aes(x = component, y = eigenvalue)) +
  geom_col(fill = irw_blue, alpha = 0.7, width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  facet_wrap(~label, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x       = "Component",
    y       = "Eigenvalue",
    caption = "Dashed line at 1 (Kaiser criterion)."
  )
```


**What to notice.** A clearly unidimensional instrument shows one eigenvalue
well above the rest, with a sharp elbow. A multidimensional instrument shows
multiple eigenvalues above 1, with a more gradual decline. The threshold is
conventional rather than principled, which is what makes Holland's result
attractive in theory: rank is a sharper notion than "above 1".

In practice the attraction does not survive contact with the estimator. The rank
claim is about $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$'s off-diagonals with the diagonal free, and
Section 3 shows what it takes to test even $D = 1$ — a weighted rank-1 fit to the
off-diagonals plus a simulated reference distribution, because the eigenvalue
count has no power and the share has no interpretable scale without one. Doing
that for general $D$ means minimum-rank fitting at each candidate rank with a
reference distribution for each, on a model that needs all $2^J$ cells. For the
$J$ at which instruments are actually screened for dimensionality, the SOE cannot
be fitted at all. The correlation-matrix scree above is the pragmatic tool; the
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ result is a statement about what dimensionality *means*
rather than a procedure for measuring it.

---

## Section 6: How many parameters does a long test support?

@holland1990dutch establishes a **conservation law**: a $D$-dimensional test of
$J$ items supports at most $(D+1)J$ parameters as $J \to \infty$. For $D = 1$
this means at most $2J$ parameters — exactly what the 2PL provides. The 3PL has
$3J$ parameters, exceeding the limit. Holland's prediction is therefore that
**the marginal gain from 2PL → 3PL should shrink as $J$ grows**, and may
become negative (overfitting) for long tests.

We test this using the InterModel Vigorish [IMV; see also @holland1990dutch] — a
log-score measure of predictive improvement — across IRW datasets spanning a
range of test lengths.

```{r}
#| label: fig-conservation
#| fig-cap: "IMV gain from 1PL → 2PL (blue) and 2PL → 3PL (red) as a function of test length J. Holland's conservation law predicts the 2PL → 3PL gain shrinks toward zero as J grows."
#| fig-height: 4.5

cons_df <- s6 |>
  filter(!is.na(imv_1v2)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(imv_1v2, imv_2v3),
    names_to  = "comparison",
    values_to = "imv"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(imv)) |>
  mutate(
    comparison = recode(
      comparison,
      imv_1v2 = "1PL → 2PL  (free discrimination)",
      imv_2v3 = "2PL → 3PL  (add guessing)"
    )
  )

ggplot(cons_df, aes(x = J, y = imv, colour = comparison)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0, alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, alpha = 0.15, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "1PL → 2PL  (free discrimination)" = irw_blue,
      "2PL → 3PL  (add guessing)"        = irw_red
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    x       = "Number of items (J)",
    y       = "IMV gain",
    caption = paste0(
      "Based on ", n_distinct(s6$table_name[!is.na(s6$imv_1v2)]),
      " IRW datasets. 3PL fitted for J ≤ 20 only."
    )
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**What to notice.** The 1PL → 2PL gain (blue) is typically positive and stable
across $J$: freeing discrimination improves fit regardless of test length,
consistent with real variation in item discriminations. The 2PL → 3PL gain (red)
should, if Holland is right, trend toward zero as $J$ grows. If it remains
positive at large $J$, that suggests genuine multidimensionality or pervasive
guessing. The pattern across the IRW is the empirical verdict.

---

::: {.callout-warning}
## Limitations

**Pattern sparsity.** Sections 1–3 require $J \leq 10$ for pattern enumeration
to be feasible. The SOE loglinear approach does not generalise to large $J$.

**Normal ability assumption.** The quadratic $\log \pi_k$ result (Section 4)
holds asymptotically under normality; skewed or multimodal ability distributions
can mimic the pattern for the wrong reasons.

**3PL instability.** The 3PL is difficult to estimate for short tests and small
samples. IMV values for 2PL → 3PL should be interpreted cautiously for $J < 10$.

**Dataset selection.** `irw_filter()` conditions are heuristic. The
"unidimensional" and "complex" candidates in Section 5 were selected on
eigenvalue structure alone. Users with substantive knowledge of specific IRW
tables should override the automatic selection.
:::

## Reproducibility

{{< include ../components/_source-links.qmd >}}

{{< include ../components/_data-version.qmd >}}

Results were computed on `r format(date_run, "%B %d, %Y")` with
`irw` version `r irw_pkg_version`. To regenerate:

```r
# 1. Re-run the compute script (from the project root)
source("vignettes/dutch_identity_compute.R")

# 2. Re-render this page
quarto::quarto_render("vignettes/dutch_identity.qmd")
```

The model-fitting and Γ-diagnostic helpers live in
`vignettes/dutch_identity_helpers.R`, which `dutch_identity_compute.R` sources.
`vignettes/dutch_identity_gamma_rerun.R` updates only the Section 3 Γ
diagnostics in the cached result, refitting the loglinear models from the stored
pattern counts and asserting that Table 1 is unchanged, so a figure fix does not
require re-running the corpus-wide sections.

The corpus sweep behind @fig-gapshare-corpus is a separate, slower job:
`vignettes/dutch_identity_gapshare.R` fits the three models to every eligible
IRW table and writes one row per table to
`vignettes/dutchdata/gapshare_tables.csv`, which is what this page reads.
`vignettes/dutch_identity_gapshare_report.R` turns that CSV into
`gapshare_summary.md` with the full breakdown, the exclusion counts and the
diagnosed outliers. Both pin the IRW version they ran against and cache per
table, so the sweep resumes rather than restarting.

::: {.callout-tip}
To cite the IRW datasets used, run:

```r
for (tbl in unique(c(s1_3$table_name, s4$rasch_meta$table_name,
                      s5$unidim$table_name, s5$multidim$table_name,
                      s6$table_name))) {
  irw_save_bibtex(tbl, output_file = "vignettes/dutchdata/irw_references.bib",
                  append = TRUE)
}
```
:::
